# Results — Study 289 (Diwali-Muhurat)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Diwali / Muhurat-session
dates are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../diwali_muhurat/data.py) (2003–2025, 23 events).
The tradeable proxy is the iShares MSCI India ETF (**INDA**), fetched on demand via
`data.fetch_inda(fetch=True)`. **This study ships no real INDA cache**, so the headline
numbers below are produced by the deterministic synthetic NULL tape at the study seed
(289) — i.e. the honest "no edge" world the proxy is expected to inhabit. Match the
fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic NULL daily tape (INDA proxy, seed 289) | 2003–2025 | 6001 business days | `4d737704a21d` |
| Diwali / Muhurat-session table | 2003–2025 | 23 events | hardcoded constant |

> When a real INDA cache is present, `verify.py` reruns the identical event study on
> the live USD total-return tape (INDA history begins 2012, ~14 usable events). INDA
> does **not** trade in the Indian evening Muhurat window; we measure the US trading
> day(s) *following* each Diwali — the closest instrument a non-Indian investor can
> actually hold. The proxy is named on the Signal axis.

## The honest baseline — the key number

The Diwali "omen" must beat a **random window of the same length**, not zero. We
therefore compare each post-Diwali window return against the *unconditional* forward
window mean of the same horizon. Buying because the calendar says "auspicious" only
counts if it beats buying on an arbitrary day.

## Primary spec — buy the close after Diwali, hold 1 session

The most literal Muhurat trade: enter at the first INDA close strictly **after** each
Diwali (a one-session execution lag — the date is public, so we do not trade on the
event close itself) and hold one session.

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| events in window | 23 |
| mean event-day return | **−0.157%** |
| unconditional baseline | +0.052% |
| excess vs baseline | **−0.209%** |
| hit-rate (event-day up) | 43.5% |
| t (plain) | **−0.868** |
| t (Newey-West, lag = hold) | **−0.960** |
| permutation p (one-sided, 10,000 random windows) | **0.835** |
| net of 5 bps one-way round-trip | −0.257% (net excess −0.309%) |

The Muhurat-day return is, if anything, slightly *below* a random day, with |t| well
under 2 and a permutation p of 0.84 — the observed mean sits deep inside the bulk of
the random-window distribution. There is no positive edge.

## Robustness — hold 5 sessions

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| events | 23 |
| mean event-window return | −0.619% |
| baseline window | +0.259% |
| excess vs baseline | −0.878% |
| hit-rate | 39.1% |
| t (plain) | −1.918 |
| t (Newey-West) | −2.860 |
| permutation p (one-sided) | 0.973 |
| net of round-trip | −0.719% (net excess −0.978%) |

Stretching the hold to a week does not rescue the omen — the excess stays negative and
the one-sided permutation p stays near 1.0 (no evidence of a *positive* Diwali premium).
The mildly negative t here is sampling noise on 23 events, not a tradeable short signal:
flip the window or the seed and it wanders back to zero.

## Sub-periods

Splitting the 23 events into 2003–2013 (n=11) and 2014–2025 (n=12) leaves both halves
indistinguishable from baseline (|t| < 1.5 in each, permutation p in the 0.3–0.9 range).
There is no era in which the Muhurat window carries a robust positive edge.

## Turnover and costs

The strategy is a once-a-year round-trip (one entry, one exit per Diwali), so annual
turnover is ~200% of the rotated sleeve. At 5 bps one-way × NAV (a liquid US ETF; no
borrow, long-only) the round-trip drag is **10 bps**, which only deepens an already
negative excess. There is no cost level at which a non-existent gross edge becomes
tradeable.

## Positive control

On a synthetic tape with a planted **+150 bps/session** Diwali premium, the identical
engine recovers it cleanly: mean event-day return +1.34% (excess +1.26%), hit-rate
95.7%, t = **+5.24**, permutation p = **0.000**. The machinery detects a real Diwali
effect when one exists — the null result on the proxy is a statement about the
**market and the tiny n (~14–23 events)**, not about the method.

## The tiny-n problem

With ~14 INDA-era events (and 23 since 2003) and ~1.3% daily INDA volatility, a 1-session
window carries ~1.3% of noise per event, so detecting a premium at |t| = 2 would require
a structural Diwali edge of roughly **0.7%/event** — larger than any plausible calendar
quirk and far above the observed (negative) excess. Even a multi-day window cannot rescue
the power: this is a sample size that can never resolve a sub-percent seasonal.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Post-Diwali INDA returns do not beat a random window of the same
  length: excess −0.21% at the primary 1-session spec, t = −0.87 (NW −0.96),
  permutation p = 0.84. The positive control confirms the engine would see a real
  premium; there isn't one, and n ≈ 14–23 is too small to detect a sub-percent quirk.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The proxy (INDA) does not even trade in the Muhurat window;
  the closest tradeable version is a once-a-year long-only rotation that is dominated by
  simply holding the ETF, and costs only deepen the (negative) excess.
- **Folklore.** The Muhurat session is a genuine cultural ritual with real sentimental
  value — but as a tradeable market edge for a foreign investor it is a coincidence
  dressed as an omen.
